case_title: Barku Bhavrao Bhaskar v. State of Maharashtra
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (related to the victim's family); prior dispute over wages between the accused and the victim's father
evidence_type: Circumstantial (last seen together, extra-judicial confession, recovery of blood-stained shirt and body, motive); medical (post-mortem); recovery evidence
confession: Extra-judicial confession made on the way back to the village, stating he killed the child over the wage dispute; treated as circumstance (ii) by the courts below and upheld by the Supreme Court
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under ss.364, 302 and 201 IPC; life imprisonment for s.302; five years RI (stated as s.354); three years RI for s.201; fine with default sentence
high_court_outcome: Appeal (Criminal Appeal No.1024 of 2001) dismissed; conviction and sentence confirmed
neutral_facts: The victim, a female child of about six years, was the daughter of a man who did masonry work. The accused was related to the victim's family and had worked for the victim's father on occasions. A dispute existed between them over wages the accused had received for work he did not perform. On the day of the incident, a witness saw the accused with the victim at the family home at around 10.30 am, with the child seated on his lap. A shopkeeper later saw the accused buy sweets for the child at about 1.15 pm. When the child could not be found that evening, the family searched the accused's house and a nearby village without success. Another child reported seeing the accused taking the victim away, but that child did not testify. Later the accused was brought back to the village by the victim's father. On the way he reportedly said that if he was not beaten he would tell the truth, and stated that he had killed the child over the wage dispute and hidden her body under stones on a mountain. At his instruction, police and witnesses went to the spot in a jeep, where the body was recovered from under stones and branches. It showed bleeding head and ear injuries, and the child was wearing a school uniform. At the accused's instruction a blood-stained shirt was recovered from under a stone on a road, and it bore blood of the same group as the victim. The accused was physically examined and had no injuries. A post-mortem found head injuries that the doctor considered antemortem and homicidal, with the cause of death being shock from cardio-respiratory arrest due to head injuries.
physical_harm: Death of the victim caused by head injuries: abrasions to face and head, scalp haematoma, skull fracture, and meningeal tears
motive: Wage/payment dispute between the accused and the victim's father (accepted by the courts below and the Supreme Court as proved)
key_evidence_accepted: Last-seen evidence of PW-3 (mother) and PW-7 (shopkeeper); extra-judicial confession; blood-stained shirt recovered at accused's instance with blood of same group as victim; body recovered at accused's instance; post-mortem evidence of PW-6; motive evidence of PWs 1, 4 and 5
witness_credibility: PW-3 found to have no reason to lie; PW-6 doctor's evidence treated as ruling out an accidental fall; motive witnesses' variations found trivial; child witness's silence not held against prosecution
post_offence_conduct: Led police to the body and to the hidden blood-stained shirt; made an extra-judicial confession
trial_duration: offence: 03.12.2000; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 10.02.2006; Supreme Court: 25.07.2013
legal_representation: Appellant: P.C. Aggarwala, Revathy Raghavan. State/Respondent: Sachin J. Patil, Sanjay V. Kharde, Asha Gopalan Nair
investigation_status: Complaint lodged at police station; recoveries of body and shirt made; post-mortem conducted; trial completed with conviction
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted and sentenced. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence confirmed. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
defence_argument: Doubts whether death was homicidal (suggestion of fall or accident); blood group of accused not tested; last-seen witness PW-7 came to light only through an unexamined person; variations in motive witnesses' versions
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence: the chain of circumstances must be complete and consistent only with guilt, with no missing link
